articles.title: What could make Milton Keynes the next City of Culture?
articles.summary: Milton Keynes is battling Wrexham, Sheffield and Blackpool for the illustrious £10m prize.
articles.body:
It's a big week for Milton Keynes as it battles with Wrexham, Sheffield and Blackpool for the illustrious £10m prize of 2029 City of Culture.

A panel of judges, including the creator of Grange Hill and Brookside, Sir Phil Redmond, are visiting the city before making a decision on the winner in the new year.

Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said: "Every place has a story worth telling of its own unique history, identity and contribution. It has been amazing to see this year's bidders showcase what makes their community claim such a special place in our national story."

So, what will judges discover that makes Milton Keynes so unique?

The moment you drive past the welcome to Milton Keynes signs, you are told it is "Different by Design".

Turning 60 on 23 January 2027, it was the last and largest of the new towns built in the 1960s before being awarded city status as part of the Queen's Platinum Jubilee celebrations in 2022.

Well, it was built around a quiet Buckinghamshire village of the same name after the then housing minister, Anthony Greenwood, gave permission to transform an 8,850-hectare area into a town for 250,000 people.

That figure has passed 300,000 and is expected to top 400,000 by 2050.

Its city centre has an American feel, with streets called boulevards and a grid system of 11 north-south and 10 east-west roads to help motorists get around, while its 200-mile (320km) network of shared paths, known as redways, keeps runners, walkers and cyclists away from traffic.

Milton Keynes has 15 lakes, and if you live there, you are never more than half a mile away from one of its 40 parks. There have been about 22 million trees planted there, and it has more bridges than Venice, many of them built over its 11 miles of canals.

More than two-thirds of the borough of Milton Keynes is countryside, although with around 2,000 new homes being built each year, that figure will diminish, especially as it has been earmarked as a potential New Town site by the government.

It is a city that prides itself on being forward-thinking with a fleet of Starship delivery robots , plus self-driving cars and buses are regularly tested on its streets, and it is part of a national e-scooter trial.

Judges will examine the community identity of each city, with Milton Keynes being a place where more than 150 languages are spoken in its schools, and Office for National Statistics data in 2021 showed 37.8% of its residents identified as Black, Asian or Minority Ethnic compared with a national average of 26.5%.

A key cultural hub is Campbell Park, which was designed by architects in the 1970s to match the exact path of the rising sun during the summer solstice and was named after Jock Campbell, who played a big part in developing the city as chairman of the Milton Keynes Development Corporation.

It has hosted events including India Day, the African Diaspora Foundation Festival, Pride, Oktoberfest and Eid, while its open-air theatre has welcomed performers such as Steps, Paloma Faith and Will Young. Its International Festival, which attracts over 90,000 visitors a year, will return in 2027.

Campbell Park is home to the Parks Trust charity that cares for more than 6,000 acres of green spaces, and its cricket ground has hosted professional games involving Northamptonshire Cricket Club.

The Milton Keynes Dons football team was founded in 2004 following Wimbledon FC's controversial relocation to the city from south London. It moved to its current 30,000-seater home in 2007 and has hosted UEFA Women's Euro 2022 matches, including the semi-final, and games in the 2015 Men's Rugby World Cup.

The judges could also test their knees on the two 220ft (67m) high indoor slopes at the Snozone, which are topped up with fresh snow each day, or visit Olney to discover the history of the famous women-only pancake race, which has been run, on and off, since 1445.

With TV legend Redmond on the judging panel, each city's creative output will be key.

In its centre, Milton Keynes Theatre opened in 1999, and its auditorium ceiling can be lowered or raised depending on the scale of the production. The MK Gallery next door has opened a four-month exhibition celebrating the life of British artist L.S. Lowry.

Beyond Campbell Park, the city hits the right musical notes thanks to the National Bowl and The Stables.

The Bowl's grass amphitheatre has a 65,000 capacity and has hosted music legends like Bon Jovi, Eminem and Oasis. Meanwhile, The Stables, founded by the late Sir John Dankworth and his wife, Dame Cleo Laine, has become the city's premier live-music venue.

The Point was the first multiplex cinema in Britain, but a campaign to make it a listed building failed, so it will be demolished and replaced by nearly 500 flats.

Milton Keynes has also appeared on the big screen, featuring in films, including Superman IV: The Quest For Peace, Withnail and I and The Imitation Game.

Mention of The Imitation Game raises another factor the judges will consider: the people, buildings and history that helped shape Milton Keynes.

During World War Two, 10,000 people, including Alan Turing, worked in secret at Bletchley Park to decode enemy communications. Their work included Colossus, the world's first programmable electronic computer.

Since 1865, the Royal train has been housed at Wolverton, and although that connection will reach the end of the line in 2027 , the transport links continue with Aston Martin cars being built in Newport Pagnell and Red Bull Racing, which has been based in the city since 1998.

While Jennie Lee was not born in Milton Keynes, her role in bringing the Open University to the city has inspired a statue in her memory.

Established by a Royal Charter in 1969 following a white paper Lee produced, it has allowed more than 2m people to study through long-distance learning.

Reverend John Newton, who lived in Olney, wrote the Amazing Grace poem, while 2012 Olympic Gold medal-winning long jumper Greg Rutherford grew up and still lives in the city.

It was the first place to introduce kerbside recycling in the UK and is home to more than 10,000 businesses, including WD40, which has its UK office in Milton Keynes. The formula for WD40, which is a the rust preventive lubricant, is a closely-guarded secret.

articles.title: Akshay Kumar, Karan Johar come out in support of Deepika Padukone's 8-hour shift demand: 'She’s earned that right, she’s a hardworking woman, a mother and a wife'
articles.summary: Filmmaker Karan Johar has come out in support of Deepika Padukone’s demand for an eight-hour workday, saying that actors have every right to set
articles.body: Filmmaker Karan Johar has come out in support of Deepika Padukone’s demand for an eight-hour workday, saying that actors have every right to set boundaries around their professional commitments. Questioning why her decision has attracted so much attention, Karan said female actors should enjoy the same flexibility as their male counterparts. During his conversation on 'Koffee with Karan' Season 9, he also praised Akshay Kumar for his discipline and commitment to work, highlighting the actor’s early-morning routine and professionalism.The discussion comes amid the ongoing debate over Deepika’s demand for fixed working hours, which became a talking point following her exit from two major projects — Sandeep Reddy Vanga’s 'Spirit' and the sequel to Nag Ashwin’s 'Kalki 2898 AD'. Akshay, who shared Karan’s views on the subject, also endorsed the importance of maintaining disciplined and time-bound shooting schedules.Speaking about his experience of working with Akshay Kumar, Karan recalled how the actor’s dedication often gets overshadowed by rumours surrounding his early-morning routine. He said that Akshay’s professionalism extends beyond his punctuality and includes his commitment to the director and producer.“When I did my first film with Akshay, there was always talks making the rounds that Akshay Kumar does this, Akshay Kumar does that. Firstly, I’ve never seen a man work this hard. He has meetings at 5 am. He knows his script by heart, and he’s always supportive of the director and very cognizant of the producer. And he’s the only superstar that gives a chance to a debut director, and that’s one thing that he doesn’t get enough credit for,” Karan shared.Taking the conversation beyond Akshay’s work ethic, Karan spoke about the need for equal treatment when it comes to actors deciding their working hours. He said he respects Deepika’s decision to seek an eight-hour shift and believes there is no reason for her demand to be treated differently.“And I think that’s exactly my point—as a producer, I respect it. And that’s why I also respect Deepika Padukone’s decision. When she says something like this, I don’t know why it’s made into such a big deal. It’s her right. She’s earned that right. She’s a hardworking woman. She’s a mother, she’s a wife, she’s a professional, and she has a personal life. Why can’t she ask for it when you ask for it? There is sometimes this gender disparity that happens, and it’s not fair. I think if a male superstar can ask for it, so can a female superstar. Any actor can ask for it. Nobody’s putting a gun on my head to sign Deepika Padukone or Akshay Kumar. I want to sign these actors because I love their work. I respect their achievement,” Karan stated.Akshay Kumar agreed with Karan’s argument, supporting the idea of eight-hour shifts and stressing that structured working schedules can benefit the entire film crew without compromising the creative process.The issue gained prominence in May 2025 when reports emerged that Deepika had walked out of 'Spirit' following reported differences with the makers over working hours and other professional conditions. A few months later, Vyjayanthi Movies announced that the actress would not be associated with the sequel to 'Kalki 2898 AD', stating that the two sides had been unable to find a partnership.Deepika later addressed the criticism surrounding her demand, maintaining that an eight-hour workday was a reasonable expectation. She also pointed out that several male superstars had been following similar schedules for years without their working hours becoming a subject of public debate.In an interview with Brut India, Deepika Padukone said, “In the Indian film industry, there are a lot of male actors who have been working on an 8-hour shift for years, and it has never made headlines. I don’t think what I am asking for is ridiculously unfair. I think only someone who has worked in the system enough will know the conditions that we work in. I am saying this as if I may say so…a top star. Imagine what the working conditions must be like for everyone else in the crew.”She reiterated her stand in a conversation with CNBC-TV18, saying, “By virtue of being a woman if that’s coming across as being pushy or whatever, then so be it. But it is no secret that a lot of superstars, male superstars in the Indian film industry have been working for 8 hours for years and it’s never made headlines.”The upcoming episode of 'Koffee with Karan' Season 9 will feature Akshay Kumar alongside actor-politician Ravi Kishan. The makers recently unveiled a promo showing the two sharing light-hearted moments, with Ravi even teaching Akshay some of his viral dance steps. articles.body:
SAN JUAN — Miss Turks and Caicos is a lobster, and unfortunately, one of her legs has fallen off. As she's making her way back down the catwalk at the Miss Universe pageant in the Coliseo de Puerto Rico, a stagehand discreetly scampers onstage to retrieve the pereiopod — which is, of course, bejeweled.

Meanwhile, the X-shaped stage fills up with other flora, fauna and symbols of national beauty. Miss Cayman Islands, whose costume is so unwieldy she appears to be a fall risk, is a swallowtail butterfly. Costa Rica is a flower with a frog on it.

We're here at the Olympics of beauty, which on Tuesday night will select one of 116 women from around the world to be its 2026 queen. This is a highly consequential year, the competition's 75th anniversary — though the title "Miss Universe" is actually turning 100 (it originated in 1926 at an unrelated, defunct competition called the International Pageant of Pulchritude ). It's also a year in which the pageant is under renewed scrutiny after a cavalcade of recent scandals escaped containment in the pageant world and burst into the mainstream. There have been lawsuits, walkouts, allegations, injuries and corporate one-upsmanship — and a documentary outlining it all. The new Miss Universe will be expected to glide above it, undertaking a year of public appearances and charity work, buoyed by a six-figure prize.

But before we get into all of that, we're birdwatching. Because on this particular night — the competition where the delegates (pageant parlance rejects the term "contestants") must wear an elaborate costume to represent their country, one that often veers into high camp — there are so many birds.

Both Miss Mexico and Miss Kenya have dressed as flamingoes. Germany is an eagle, and Ireland is two swans. Namibia is something called a southern Carmine bee-eater, and Miss Nicaragua, who emerges to deafening screams, has doves with mechanical flapping wings perched over her shoulders.

Other countries have chosen a more conceptual route. Miss Romania is a Constantin Brâncuși sculpture. Miss Finland is the embodiment of " sisu , a Finnish word that translates to inner strength," per the announcers, and, sure, we suppose inner strength looks like a sparkly gown with a thigh-high slit and a cape. Miss Italy has swathed herself in Dante's "The Divine Comedy" — one side of her cape is Inferno; the other side is Paradiso. Miss Norway, who is known for really committing to the bit — last year, the country's titleholder was a fileted salmon — has decided to be a mountain troll.

And then there's our hometown girl. That would be Miss USA Justus Kelley, 31, who hails from Alexandria, Virginia: the first married woman and first mother to compete in Miss Universe for the United States, after a recent rule change. She marches on stage in a spangly corset surrounded by a halo of newspaper headlines celebrating that achievement, and honoring others in women's history: Rosa Parks refusing to give up her seat, Sally Ride's journey to space, women's suffrage.

"As a woman who made history with this title," she tells The Washington Post, "that's who I want to represent — women that came before me that were the first to do things."

Three weeks ago, Kelley had still been living a relatively normal life in her modest Alexandria townhome, which was full of kid apparatus — high chairs and bottle drying racks for her two foster toddlers — when she led a reporter inside to chat. Until recently, she hadn't even taken time off from her job as a fundraiser for St. Jude's Children's Hospital. She has eschewed one of her prizes — a Miami apartment — preferring to minimize disruption to her childrens' lives. She runs a nonprofit called Foster Footprints, supporting children and families in the foster care system.

Kelley is not the first married woman or mother to win Miss USA. That distinction goes to Mary Leona Gage, who in 1957 was forced to relinquish her title and had to withdraw from Miss Universe. Gage went on to have a tumultuous life: financial troubles, multiple marriages and divorces, self-harm. She was "preyed on by men from an early age," her son said in her obituary . At one point, she lost custody of her children, another obituary said.

Kelley and her husband — they're college sweethearts — had long wanted to become foster parents, inspired by a college friend of hers who had aged out of the foster system and spent school breaks with Kelley's family. She and her husband are open to adopt foster children placed with them, but their goal is to reunite children with their parents. She is bound to protect the privacy of her foster children, but says that most of her placements come from families that weren't abusive, but were experiencing extreme economic hardship.

"W e're helping a family that's down and needs help, just like I would hope someone does for me," she says. "And I would really pray that if someone were helping me and watching my kids, that they weren't like, 'I hope I can keep them forever,' right? "

All of this is to say that Kelley feels ties to Gage that go beyond their sashes. So the headlines on Kelley's dress paid tribute to her, too.

"I just, I think, the least that could be done is to honor her, and honor where society should have been by then, you know, but wasn't," she says. "I'm grateful to get to be the first. But it just feels like she needs to be a part of it with me."

Miss Universe has grown more inclusive since Gage's days, but it's also waned in influence, at least in the U.S. It used to be prime-time network television in America; it has been downgraded to the streaming service Reelz . Most Washingtonians were probably unaware that Miss USA lived and worked among them.

But here in San Juan, Kelley has been swept into a world of glamour and fandom that exceeds most contiguous American expectations. Outside the U.S. — especially in pageant-fanatic countries like the Philippines, Venezuela, and the Dominican Republic — Miss Universe delegates are national celebrities, known by name. Telemundo's coverage has been breathlessly comprehensive. Legions of fans have traveled to Puerto Rico to cheer them on. And for those that can't make it? They follow along on social media with their on-the-ground correspondents, the Missologists.

The Missologists, as they call themselves, are content creators: mostly gay men, many from Latin America and Southeast Asia, who follow the delegates' every move. The Missologists line the hotel lobby every morning with ring lights and tripods so they can stream live video of the women walking through the lobby.

The Missologists were the ones who revealed the main stage would be in the shape of an X. The Missologists broke the news that Miss Cuba had food poisoning, and that Miss France was escorted into one event in a wheelchair (she had stumbled and suffered a ligament injury, she later revealed on social media). The Missologists scream the names of the countries of the delegates as they walk by — "PARAGUAYYYYY! MACAAAUUUUUU!!!" — and capture footage of the delegates walking by and blowing kisses.

"As a blogger, we don't sleep," says Jose Sanchez, whose account, @Kikesanchez3310 , has dutifully followed every queen, and calls his coverage "a celebration of the women." He added: "We're not stalking, by the way."

Around 10:30 p.m., the delegates return from the competition via three buses that pull up to the Marriott lobby, where the throng has grown so large that each girl needs their own security escort. They aren't even able to stop and talk to their own families, who gather in the lobby too — elbowed out by the content creators — for the chance to make eye contact with their daughters, sisters and wives.

"It was her birthday on Friday," says Aislinn Howard, sister to Miss Ireland, Aideen Howard. The morning of the preliminaries, she's staked out a spot right behind the lobby barricade with her mother and some friends, who are all holding pictures of Howard's face. "We can't even give her a hug."

"El Salvador, mi amor!" yelled Sanchez, who was streaming to his 65,000 followers. "Chile! Chile bella!" On the phone of a streamer next to him, a notification pops up: "Your likes are up 2100 percent."

We probably shouldn't go any further without explaining the drama of the pageant itself. It's a lot. Buckle up.

After Donald Trump sold the pageant in 2015, it passed through the corporate hands of IMG, a talent and event production agency, before being purchased by a Thai conglomerate owned by businesswoman and transgender activist Anne Jakrajutatip . But Jakrajutatip's company filed for bankruptcy a year later, and then sold 50 percent of the pageant to a company led by Raul Rocha Cantu, a Mexican millionaire.

Within two years, both leaders would be under investigation in their respective countries. Investigators froze Rocha Cantu's accounts while he was under investigation for fuel and arms trafficking; the charges were dismissed earlier this year. Last year, Jakrajutatip was convicted of fraud and sentenced to two years in prison but failed to appear in court.

Meanwhile: Corporate Miss Universe was divided by hemisphere, with Thai media personality Nawat Itsaragrisil asserting control over the East as CEO, and Rocha's holding company, Legacy, maintaining ownership of the West. Earlier this year, the two entities began releasing statements asserting their ownership over the brand, via competing Miss Universe websites, with press releases that say things like, " The Organization does not recognize any efforts, including those undertaken through Mr. Nawat Itsaragrisil , to implement or give effect to such transaction and expressly reserves all rights and remedies available to it," and " MU East does not believe in favoritism or selective treatment ," and " MU East will not respond with personal attacks ." Which are all totally things a normal, stable organization would do.

Are you still with me? Let's go back to Itsaragrisil, who made a name for himself at last year's Miss Universe pageant for allegedly calling Miss Mexico a " dumbhead " — he has said that he was actually saying the world "damage" — spurring her and other delegates to walk out.

Then, three judges quit , alleging that the pageant had been rigged in favor of Miss Mexico, who went on to win. Then! Miss Jamaica tumbled through an opening in the stage and was injured so badly that she is still recovering. She is suing the Miss Universe Organization , alleging negligence. Many of these scandals were recapped in " Crown of Deceit ," a TLC documentary that was released last week.

But wait, there's more! Because of the East vs. West power struggle with Rocha, six candidates from countries with pageants overseen by Itsaragrisil — including pageant powerhouses like Thailand and Vietnam — have been barred from participating in this year's pageant. And because the pageant is being held in the U.S. territory of Puerto Rico, several beauty queens from countries subject to visa restrictions , including Congo and South Sudan, have been shut out of the competition.

Earlier this month, a bikini fashion show called "Beauty on the Beach" featured a runway with a platform over sand, and video after video showed delegates nearly twisting their ankles as they traversed it. The Miss Universe Organization issued a press release saying that the event was independently organized and "did not meet the standards of excellence and professionalism that the Miss Universe Organization expects."

Finally: Miss Universe East announced that next year's Miss Universe pageant will take place in Vietnam. Miss Universe West announced that the true location of next year's pageant, which will not be Vietnam, will be announced at Tuesday's final competition.

Okay. Whew. Now that we've explained the anxious undercurrent going into this week's events, we can get back to what really matters: The outfits.

Before she left, Kelley received a 17-page document from Miss Universe that outlined everything she and fellow delegates must do and pack before arrival. It asks that the delegates "keep your wardrobe to a reasonable amount" before proceeding to outline 48 mandatory outfits for 20 different locations, complete with required colors, that every woman must bring. Many bring more. "Animal print is absolutely NOT allowed" the document blares, in red font. It all costs a spectacular amount of money, though it can be offset by brand deals and a wardrobe subsidy from winning their country's crown.

Do the most, but not too much : It's a mixed message that made me think about what we were all doing here, at a competition named with such grandiosity that it purports to select the most beautiful life-form in the entire universe (needless to say, the human species seems to be wildly overrepresented). Back when Mary Leona Gage was denied her shot at the crown, becoming Miss Universe only required conventional good looks, a slim body, a lack of marital or juvenile dependents, and a lot of charm. Today, it's so much more.

The women of Miss Universe perform acts of cultural diplomacy and are beholden to even more expectations than a politician, but wield no political power (something Miss Israel experienced acutely during the costume contest, when she wore a cape emblazoned with the word "Peace" in English, Hebrew, and Arabic, and was booed by some in the crowd).

"I've just I've been a part of some really, really great conversations with girls where we acknowledge, you know, we love our countries," says Kelley. "That doesn't mean that we are our governments, right?" She felt "a weight" knowing that other delegates were shut out of the competition because of her country's visa policies.

"We are here connecting as people," says Kelley. "The first thing I look at is not a person's sash."

During the preliminary competition, when all 116 delegates get their turn to show off their swimsuit and their evening gown, announcers detailed each woman's accomplishments: master's degrees from Cambridge, NGOs created to save children from homelessness, fluency in five languages, companies founded.

Becoming Miss USA, Kelley said in her final answer during that pageant, meant "no longer questioning if we have to choose between our ambitious careers, our families, and our wildest dreams." Women can have it all.

But Miss Universe is a representation of the ideal woman, and if the ideal woman wants to have it all, she also has no choice but to do it all.

She must have a perfect body, perfect teeth, perfect hair. She needs the right answer to every question, and must never make any gaffes. She cannot be too opinionated, but also cannot be too generic. She has to do charity work (children, animals, nothing too political) and walk in 6-inch heels. She has to be smart. These days, she has to be a content creator with a large following. She can be a mom. She can be an entrepreneur. She can be an NCAA bowler who once bowled a perfect 300 (Miss Jordan) or a communications professional working in the office of her country's prime minister (Miss Trinidad and Tobago).

She must be fresh-faced in the lobby each morning with a full face of makeup and a gown, eagerly greeting the throngs addressing her as only a country, not a person with a name. After only getting four hours of sleep each night. And wearing heels every day for three weeks straight. And wearing a lobster costume. And being away from your toddlers. And offering yourself up for subjective judgement by an official panel and a faceless internet mob.

She can do all of these things perfectly, and still lose.

There are certainly easier ways to get famous, or launch a modeling career, or get thousands of Instagram followers. But the title of Miss Universe still holds a unique appeal. Maybe that's the "wildest dreams" part of what Kelley referenced in her final answer.

Back in Kelley's Alexandria townhouse three weeks before the competition, she's pondering this. And she offers an analogy from Mahjong , a game she recently started playing.

The objective, which involves both luck and skill, is to form certain winning combinations of tiles. She recently experienced a "moment of things clicking and feeling like, man, what's happening right now in the game is how life feels. And I had a really good hand and I was so excited about everything, but it was time to discard something," she says. She didn't want to, but the rules meant she had to. "It's time to let something go. "

So when she thinks about what it would mean to win Miss Universe, she's ready with another perfect pageant answer.

" C oming into this, I knew very early on: My goal might not be to win. My goal is to make sure people know there's nearly half a million kids in foster care," she says. "So I think it's so cool to leave that experience having won, but this, to me, is what's most important. "

articles.title: Parvathy Thiruvothu on ADHD, career slowdown and decision to hustle like never before: ‘You may fail, but fail gloriously’
articles.summary: Actress Parvathy Thiruvothu is currently experiencing one of the busiest phases of her career, taking on multiple projects and exploring a variety of
articles.body: Actress Parvathy Thiruvothu is currently experiencing one of the busiest phases of her career, taking on multiple projects and exploring a variety of roles. After spending nearly two decades in the film industry, the actress decided to push herself out of her comfort zone and embrace new opportunities. In a recent conversation with actress and television presenter Ranjini Haridas, Parvathy opened up about this change in her approach to work, her decision to take more risks and how living with ADHD influences her perception of time.Speaking on Ranjini Haridas' YouTube channel, Parvathy agreed that this has been one of the fastest and busiest phases of her professional life in almost 20 years. Recalling how her work schedule looked a few years ago, she spoke about filming 'Ullozhukku' and 'Dhootha' in 2022, followed by spending around 75 days shooting for 'Thangalaan' in 2023. However, she decided to change her approach to work and challenge herself to explore more opportunities.Explaining the mindset that prompted this shift, Parvathy said, “The next three years, let's hustle like you've never done before. You're not gonna die, okay? You may fail, but fail gloriously. Reserve the right to fail at it. Maybe you'll fall apart in ways you'll be put together differently, but do it.” She added that she wanted to find inspiration and opportunities for growth within herself rather than constantly looking for them outside.The actress also clarified that taking up more work does not mean accepting projects indiscriminately. She has been consciously choosing stories and characters that challenge her as an actor. Speaking about her experience of working with women filmmakers, she expressed how their projects have pushed her creatively and emotionally.Opening up about living with ADHD and how it affects her relationship with time, Parvathy said, “I have ADHD, but I am not one of those who want to make a big point out of it. I feel like time works in a different way for me. Time has elasticity; therefore, I can stretch time if need be. However, it doesn’t mean that I won’t sleep. I will certainly do that."The actress has previously spoken about how she would follow rigid routines after completing a film shoot, often preferring to withdraw from social interactions. However, she said her approach to life outside work has also evolved, allowing her to embrace new experiences and a more flexible routine.On the work front, Parvathy has had a busy 2026, with projects including 'Tu Yaa Main', 'I, Nobody' alongside Prithviraj Sukumaran and the crime thriller 'Pradhama Drishtiya Kuttakkar'. She is also set to headline the upcoming web series 'Storm', directed by Ajitpal Singh and produced by Hrithik Roshan and Eshaan Roshan. The series also features Alaya F, Srishti Shrivastava, Rrama Sharma and Saba Azad.Her upcoming projects also include the second season of 'Dhootha' with Naga Chaitanya and 'Captain India', starring Kartik Aaryan and directed by Shimit Amin.Get the latest Bollywood & Entertainment News, and more. articles.title: Sooraj Barjatya drops update on ‘Prem Ki Shaadi’ with Salman Khan: 'Abhi thoda sa waqt aur hai...'
articles.summary: Sooraj Barjatya is all set to release his new film, ‘Yeh Prem Mol Liya’, starring Ayushmann Khurrana and Sharvari.
articles.body: Sooraj Barjatya is all set to release his new film, ‘Yeh Prem Mol Liya’, starring Ayushmann Khurrana and Sharvari. Anupam Kher, Supriya Pathak, Seema Pahwa, Saumya Tandon, Shaad Randhawa and Swanand Kirkire play key supporting roles, and the film arrives in theatres on November 27. In the meantime, fans are also eagerly anticipating the filmmaker's long-awaited reunion with Salman Khan in ‘Prem Ki Shaadi’.Sooraj Barjatya on 'Prem Ki Shaadi' updateThe filmmaker has now given an update on where the project stands. Speaking to The Free Press Journal, he said, "Abhi thoda sa wakht aur hai, kyunki thoda aur mujhe kuch cheezein polish karni hai." His words hint that the filmmaker is taking some more time to fine-tune a few elements before moving ahead with the film.Salman Khan to play Prem again in 'Prem Ki Shaadi'Barjatya revealed at a 2022 screening of ‘Uunchai’ in Mumbai that he was working on another film with Salman Khan. He mentioned that the title ‘Prem Ki Shaadi’ was already registered, and Salman then announced the name publicly. The actor also confirmed that he would play his beloved character Prem once again, this time tying the knot on screen.Salman Khan and Sooraj Barjatya's films togetherSalman Khan's rise to stardom began with Sooraj Barjatya's 1989 romantic drama ‘Maine Pyar Kiya’, in which he appeared alongside Bhagyashree. The actor and filmmaker have since reunited for crowd-pleasers like ‘Hum Aapke Hain Koun’ (1994), ‘Hum Saath Saath Hain’ (1999) and ‘Prem Ratan Dhan Payo’ (2015). articles.title: Billy Ray Cyrus shares heartfelt tribute to Miley Cyrus after her wedding to Maxx Morando: 'Proudest dad alive'
articles.summary: Billy Ray Cyrus and his partner, actor Elizabeth Hurley, attended Miley Cyrus' wedding in Palm Springs on Saturday.
articles.body:
Billy Ray Cyrus has shared a heartfelt birthday tribute to daughter Miley Cyrus following her wedding.

The "Flowers" singer married music producer Maxx Morando on Saturday in Palm Springs, Calif., after five years together.

Billy Ray and his partner, actor Elizabeth Hurley, were among the guests at the star-studded ceremony, as well as Hurley's son, Damian. Miley has previously acknowledged that she and her dad have had challenges in their relationship in the past .

Sharing wedding snapshots on Instagram, the country musician said he was "the proudest dad alive" after his daughter "married the love of her life."

The photo carousel opens with a black-and-white image of Billy Ray dancing with Miley, her head resting on his shoulder, and features shots from the wedding, including what appears to be Miley and her husband exchanging vows during the ceremony, which was reportedly officiated by the Flaming Lips' singer Wayne Coyne.

The final slide is a throwback to Miley as a child, in which she winks at the camera in a visor reading "Billy Ray Cyrus 10th Anniversary" and a "Rock Star" tank top.

Addressing his daughter, who turned 34 on Monday, Billy Ray wrote that "words can't begin to express how proud you make me every day," and told Morando he was "so honored to welcome you to the family."

He added that the couple was "a match made in heaven" and that he "can't wait to keep celebrating you both today and forever."

In the caption, which also wished Miley a happy birthday, Billy Ray said he "can't describe how beautiful it felt to have all my family together in one room, united by love."

Hurley showed her support and commented on the post with "Love you 🩷", while her son Damian wrote: "Love you so much, BRC ❤️"

Rumors of a rift between Billy Ray and Miley began when Tish Cyrus filed for divorce from Billy Ray in 2022 after 30 years of marriage. The split was said to have divided the couple's children, HELLO! Magazine reported, with Miley remaining close to her mother.

While both Billy Ray and Tish remarried — Billy Ray to singer Firerose in 2023, later divorcing her in 2024 and Tish to Prison Break actor Dominic Purcell — Miley only confirmed her attendance at her mother's ceremony.

Miley left her father out of her speech at the Grammys in February 2024, with Billy Ray later sharing a cryptic Instagram post , which has since been removed, reading "Love is the answer."

In May 2025, during a reflective interview with the New York Times , Miley shared that she was no longer estranged from her father. She said that as she's gotten older, she's come to see her parents "as individuals instead of as parents," and that seeing both of them in love has let her "love them both as individuals instead of as a parental pairing."

"At first it's hard, because the little kid in you reacts before the adult in you can go, 'Yes, that's your dad, but that's just another person that deserves to be in his bliss and to be happy.' My child self has caught up," she told the publication.

The following month, Miley appeared on the Reclaiming podcast with Monica Lewinsky to discuss her family. Recalling the breakdown, she said: "Half of us weren't speaking to each other at one point, and we cleaned all that up." Remarking on the "messy" nature of the fallout, she said: "It was easier to just go, 'white flag,'" referring to the signal for surrender.

Speaking to NPR in September 2025, Miley said her song "Secrets" was an olive branch.

"I wanted him to know that I'm grown now, and I'm a safe space for him. I'm as much a friend as I am his kid," said Cyrus. "That's what this song was really about for me. Being that place that my dad feels safe…if you don't take my hand as I reach it out, I'm going to chase you because I want that relationship in my life."

When the song was first released, Billy Ray wrote on Instagram that it was the "Best birthday gift a dad could ever ask for."

articles.title: Guru Randhawa faces police complaint and legal warning ahead of Delhi concert over alleged glorification of drugs and alcohol, gets 7-day warning
articles.summary: Singer Guru Randhawa has landed in a controversy ahead of his upcoming 'Sirra Tour' concert in New Delhi, following a police complaint and a legal warning
articles.body: Singer Guru Randhawa has landed in a controversy ahead of his upcoming 'Sirra Tour' concert in New Delhi, following a police complaint and a legal warning over the alleged glorification of drugs and alcohol in his music. The singer is scheduled to perform at Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium on December 12, 2026. The complaint reportedly raises concerns about the influence of such content on his young fan following and seeks assurances regarding the songs and performances planned for the event.Following the complaint, a formal warning email was reportedly sent to Guru Randhawa, his management team and associated music labels, including Saregama Live and Warner Music. The communication was issued by a complainant identified as Aashayein.One of the primary objections concerns references to narcotic substances in the singer's lyrics. The complainant has reportedly highlighted an earlier lyrical change in which the word "Afeem" (opium) was replaced with "Jameen". The notice questions whether the original lyrics or similar references to drugs could be included in the upcoming concert's setlist.The complainant has also raised objections to the depiction of alcohol in Guru Randhawa's song and music video 'Azul'. According to the notice, such portrayals could potentially normalise alcohol consumption among the singer's considerable young audience.Among the demands made in the complaint is a public assurance from Guru Randhawa or his authorised management through official social media platforms, including Instagram, Facebook and YouTube. The requested assurance states that ‘No lyrics or performances promoting or glorifying narcotic substances will be included in the December 12 setlist’.The complainant has further sought an assurance that there will be no promotion of drug consumption during the concert and that the artist and event organisers will comply with applicable laws and regulations.Guru Randhawa, his management team and the organisers have reportedly been given seven days to respond to the communication in writing and issue a public statement. The notice also warns that failure to comply could lead to the matter being escalated to the Narcotics Control Bureau (NCB) and other relevant authorities. It further raises the possibility of an examination of the concert's permissions and licence, which could potentially lead to restrictions, changes to the event or even its cancellation, depending on the authorities' findings and subsequent action.So far, Guru Randhawa, his representatives and the event organisers have not issued an official response to the complaint.Meanwhile, the singer has had a busy year with several independent releases and collaborations. His recent tracks include 'Marzi', 'SIX', '2 EYES', 'CSky' and 'FOSHO'. He also released 'So What' on October 27, featuring Anjini Dhawan in the music video, followed by 'Sirra (Steve Aoki Remix)' on November 6, 2026.Get the latest Bollywood & Entertainment News, and more. articles.title: BTS' V and Jungkook recreate 'Naatu Naatu' hook step; 'RRR' team reacts, says ‘The fever never stops’
articles.summary: The global popularity of 'Naatu Naatu' continues to bring Indian cinema and international music fans together.
articles.body: The global popularity of 'Naatu Naatu' continues to bring Indian cinema and international music fans together. The Oscar-winning song from SS Rajamouli's 'RRR', featuring Ram Charan and Jr NTR, has once again caught the attention of fans after BTS members V and Jungkook were seen performing its popular hook step. The film's official social media handle has now reacted to the video, thanking the K-pop stars for their love for the song.The official 'RRR' account recently shared a clip of V and Jungkook recreating the signature choreography of 'Naatu Naatu' during BTS' ARIRANG World Tour. Expressing its excitement over the duo's performance, the team wrote, "ForeveRRR!! The #NaatuNaatu fever never stops! Thank you #Taehyung and #Jungkook for the love."Watch the video hereThe post comes shortly after V spoke about his fondness for Indian cinema during an interaction with fans on Weverse. When asked about his favourite Indian films, the singer named Aamir Khan's '3 Idiots' and 'Dangal', along with 'RRR'. He also revealed that he had memorised the choreography from the Telugu blockbuster, giving Indian fans another reason to celebrate his admiration for the film.Interestingly, the video shared by the 'RRR' team is not a recent recording. It is an older clip from BTS' ARIRANG World Tour, showing V and Jungkook enjoying the popular dance number during a concert. This is not the first time a BTS member has shown an interest in the song. Jungkook had previously played 'Naatu Naatu' during a Weverse Live session in 2023, drawing attention from Indian fans and the film's team.Released in 2022, 'RRR' was directed by SS Rajamouli and featured Ram Charan and Jr NTR in the lead roles, alongside Alia Bhatt and Ajay Devgn. The period action drama emerged as a major international success, earning recognition across several global platforms.Composed by MM Keeravaani, with lyrics by Chandrabose, 'Naatu Naatu' was performed by Rahul Sipligunj and Kaala Bhairava. The energetic track, known for its distinctive hook step and demanding choreography, went on to make history by winning the Academy Award for Best Original Song at the 95th Oscars in 2023. It also won the Golden Globe for Best Original Song, further establishing its international popularity.The latest interaction between BTS and the 'RRR' team is another reminder of the song's enduring appeal, with its music and choreography continuing to find admirers across different countries and cultures.Get the latest Bollywood & Entertainment News, and more. articles.summary: Meghan Markle could be pulled into a criminal investigation involving her estranged father, according to experts. Thomas Markle Sr. was arrested on Nov. 6 in Florida.
articles.body: A criminal investigation involving Meghan Markle’s estranged father, Thomas Markle Sr., threatens to pull the Duchess of Sussex into her family’s legal troubles, according to experts. A legal expert told Fox News Digital that authorities could seek her cooperation if they believe she possesses information relevant to the allegations against her father. "She may decide to cooperate with the investigation and may agree to be interviewed, almost certainly under certain negotiated conditions," Los Angeles entertainment and trial attorney Jordan Matthews said. "If she decides not to cooperate, then she could be compelled to provide information in connection with a subpoena." Prince Harry could also be pulled into the investigation, but his communications with Meghan would likely be protected, according to Matthews. MEGHAN MARKLE SAYS SHE KEPT FATHER AWAY FROM KIDS TO 'PROTECT' THEM OVER 'DISTURBING ALLEGATIONS' AGAINST HIM "Regardless, while he may also agree to cooperate, and while they will both likely take a public stance that they will cooperate and do anything necessary to protect the rights of children — even if Harry is not actually pulled into the investigation, he has already been pulled into the public fallout," Matthews, of Holtz Matthews LLP, explained. "Meghan and Harry are both obviously not immune from negative press coverage." Fox News Digital reached out to Archewell for comment. Federal prosecutors charged Markle Sr. with one count of possessing child sexual abuse material in a criminal complaint filed Nov. 5 before he was arrested in Florida. According to the 14-page complaint obtained by Fox News Digital, FBI agents searched two storage units registered to Markle Sr. and seized approximately 78 items, including film negatives, slides and books containing suspected child sexual abuse material. Investigators say Markle Sr. had rented the units since 2008 and continued paying for them through October 2026. Agents identified approximately 18 suspected illegal images among film negatives recovered from one unit. A witness, who had known Markle Sr. since the 1970s, allegedly identified him as the adult man appearing with a prepubescent girl in at least two photographs. The complaint did not name the witness. However, reports have since surfaced that Meghan's mom played a key role in the arrest of her ex-husband. Doria Ragland helped federal agents identify Markle Sr. in photos seized in the ongoing child pornography investigation, according to People magazine. The outlet reported Meghan is prepared to assist the FBI in the investigation if needed. Ragland and Markle Sr. were married in 1979 and later divorced in 1987. The couple reportedly met in the late 1970s while working in television in Los Angeles. Markle Sr. was a lighting director, while Ragland worked as a makeup artist. Meghan was born in 1981. WATCH: MEGHAN MARKLE'S ESTRANGED FATHER RULED COMPETENT TO STAND TRIAL IN CHILD SEX ABUSE CASE Investigators believe Markle Sr. could be in his 30s or 40s in the photographs, according to The Sun. The photos reportedly could have been taken when Meghan was young or before she was born. The Philippine National Police in Cebu also filed criminal complaints on Nov. 17 accusing Markle Sr. of two counts of offering, distributing, selling, exporting or importing child sexual abuse or exploitation material, along with one count of possessing such material. Markle Sr., who faces up to 20 years in prison if convicted in the U.S., had initially been released on bail before being detained again this month after allegedly cutting off his electronic monitoring tag. On Nov. 19, a federal court deemed him mentally competent to stand trial following a court-ordered psychiatric evaluation. He is scheduled to appear for a preliminary hearing in Florida on Dec. 1. The investigation began after Markle Sr.'s son, Thomas Markle Jr., reported finding storage boxes containing suspected child sexual abuse images at his father's local residence and turned the materials over to authorities. Relatives have since claimed Markle Sr.’s trips to the region were an open family secret. Bobby Lucero, the son of Markle Sr.’s first wife, Roslyn Loveless, told The Sunday Times he grew up hearing stories from his mother and half-siblings about Markle Sr. visiting the Philippines on what they called his "girls trip." Lucero’s stepfather, Anthony Gonzales, also recalled hearing that Markle Sr. "liked young girls," though he told the outlet he never suspected at the time it involved minors. Markle Sr. previously denied the allegations against him in a statement to the Daily Mail. "I’m shocked, I’m hurt, and I’m very upset that my son is making these accusations against me," he was quoted as saying. "I could never do what I’m being accused of. It’s the worst thing anyone could accuse me of." "While Thomas Markle Sr. is presumed innocent until proven guilty and Meghan Markle hasn’t been accused of any involvement in any alleged offenses, it is nevertheless definitely tarnishing to be from such a family," British royal expert Hilary Fordwich told Fox News Digital. "Men who behave in such a manner with women so much younger forever tarnish their family." "Prosecutors could request statements, letters, or other records Meghan Markle has made, but one could anticipate differences depending on laws in the U.S., Philippines, or elsewhere," she added. "To date, there aren’t public reports of Meghan Markle being subpoenaed yet. She thus far is merely a family member who received prior allegations." "I trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families." "Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children." Fox News Digital previously reported Buckingham Palace was blindsided by Markle Sr.'s arrest. articles.body: Police are investigating a security breach at Prince William and Kate Middleton’s country home in England after intruders broke into the property on Monday night. Authorities noted that the two suspects remain in police custody and confirmed that "the property was unoccupied at the time of the incident," adding that "inquiries remain ongoing." articles.title: AICWA writes to PM Modi seeking ban on Fawad Khan and Mahira Khan's Pakistani Netflix series 'Jo Bachay Hain Sang Samait Lo' in India
articles.summary: The All India Cine Workers Association (AICWA) has written to Prime Minister Narendra Modi, seeking a complete ban on the Pakistani series 'Jo Bachay Hain
articles.body: The All India Cine Workers Association (AICWA) has written to Prime Minister Narendra Modi, seeking a complete ban on the Pakistani series 'Jo Bachay Hain Sang Samait Lo' on Netflix in India. The association has also demanded a long-term legal ban on Pakistani films, television shows and artists appearing on Indian screens. The demand comes ahead of the series' scheduled release on December 4, 2026. However, it is not yet clear whether the show will be available on Netflix in India.In a letter dated November 24, AICWA president Suresh Shyamlal Gupta appealed to the Prime Minister to ensure that the series is neither released nor streamed in India.The association shared the letter on X, stating that it had raised the matter with the Centre and that national interests should take priority over entertainment. It also urged Netflix India not to stream Pakistani content on its platform.Association refers to Pahalgam attack and 2025 OTT advisoryAICWA referred to an advisory issued by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting on May 8, 2025, asking OTT platforms and digital intermediaries in India to refrain from streaming Pakistani content following the Pahalgam terror attack.According to the association, streaming the upcoming series would go against the spirit of the government's directive.The letter also referred to AICWA's earlier stand against Pakistani artists working in Indian films following the 2019 Pulwama terror attack.Fawad Khan and Mahira Khan headline Pakistani Netflix series'Jo Bachay Hain Sang Samait Lo' is based on the bestselling novel of the same name by author Farhat Ishtiaq. The series explores multiple love stories spanning three generations and was shot in Pakistan, Italy and the United Kingdom.The show features Fawad Khan, Mahira Khan, Ahad Raza Mir, Hamza Ali Abbasi, Hania Aamir, Ahmed Ali Akbar, Bilal Ashraf, Maya Ali and Iqra Aziz.Produced by Momina Duraid Films, the series marks Netflix's first Pakistani original series. articles.title: Viral couple seen arguing on ESPN college football broadcast clear up what happened — and where they stand
articles.summary: The action on the field at the Wake Forest-Georgia Tech game on Saturday took a backseat to the drama between a young couple in the stands that was being narrated on the ESPN broadcast by none other than the host of “The Bachelor.”
articles.body: The action on the field at the Wake Forest-Georgia Tech game on Saturday took a backseat to the drama between a young couple in the stands that was being narrated on the ESPN broadcast by none other than the host of “The Bachelor.” The full cycle between an argument and a makeup kiss took place in the largely barren bleachers between Georgia Tech students Tallulah Wall and Braden Flournoy. The rollercoaster of emotions riveted viewers, becoming a viral moment while their Yellow Jackets were busy getting blown out 50-29 by the visiting Demon Deacons. The couple appeared on “TODAY” Tuesday to talk about the interaction that became one of the most memorable scenes across college football over the weekend. The two 21-year-olds said they have been dating for two months and one week, and their moment on camera doubled as a hard launch of their relationship. “A lot of our friends actually had no idea we were dating until that happened,” Flournoy told Savannah Guthrie, Jenna Bush Hager and Craig Melvin. “So not only were we getting texts, ‘Oh hey, you were on the screen for like a solid couple seconds,’ it was, ‘You have a boyfriend?’” Wall said. They learned from a stadium worker at the game that they had been plastered all over the internet. The couple also would like it stated for the record that there was no on-camera breakup, just a dispute. “Honestly, it was completely insignificant,” Flournoy said. “It was more miscommunication than anything,” he added. “Absolutely miscommunication,” Wall agreed. “So much miscommunication, that’s why we were like, ‘Let’s just go back and watch this football game even if we’re losing.’” “And to clear the air, there was zero speculation between us breaking up,” Flournoy added. As it was occurring, ESPN color analyst Jesse Palmer was analyzing everything from eye contact to body language between the two on the broadcast. Palmer has seen plenty of dramatic moments between couples in his days as host of “The Bachelor” since 2021. “This playoff situation is intense right now, maybe not as intense as this conversation though,” Palmer said on the broadcast. “I mean you’re the expert here my man, you break this down,” play-by-play announcer Joe Tessitore said to Palmer. The former Florida quarterback and one-time “Bachelor” himself even started diagramming the situation on the telestrator as the couple was arguing. “He is locked in,” Palmer said. “He is holding her to court right now. He wants an answer. They are in each other’s personal space, he’s not happy with whatever she just told him.” The cameras later returned to the couple for an update, and they were seen sharing a kiss. “That’s good news,” Palmer said. “This is great,” Tessitore said. “Embrace the love, America.” “OK, get a room though,” Palmer advised. The couple said they did not know who Palmer was until after their moment on camera. “Neither of us had ever watched ‘The Bachelor,’” Wall said. Wall and Flournoy are both fourth-year students at Georgia Tech and diehard Yellow Jackets fans. Wall studies mechanical engineering and Flournoy is a computer science major. Their hope is that their moment can light a fire under Georgia Tech football, which is in the midst of a 3-8 season, in order to keep the focus on the field instead of the action in the stands. “Brent Key please, please use this as motivation to be better at football,” Flournoy pleaded on “TODAY,” addressing the Yellow Jackets head coach. “I know I don’t have to tell you, you’re going to get fired up anyway because that’s the kind of coach you are, but please.”

articles.summary: Filmmaker Antoine Fuqua, best known for directing the Michael Jackson biopic 'Michael', has landed in legal trouble after a man accused him and his son,
articles.body: Filmmaker Antoine Fuqua, best known for directing the Michael Jackson biopic 'Michael', has landed in legal trouble after a man accused him and his son, Brando, of assaulting him at a Los Angeles bar. The man, identified as William Rosenthal, has filed a lawsuit accusing the director and his son of assault, battery and intentional infliction of emotional distress over an alleged incident in February.According to a report by the Daily Mail, Rosenthal, who worked as an assistant bar manager at Good Times at Davey Wayne's in Los Angeles, claimed that Fuqua struck him in the head with a handgun. He has also accused the filmmaker's son of pointing a gun at him during the alleged confrontation. Fuqua has strongly denied the allegations, with his representative stating that none of the claims made in the lawsuit are true.What happened at the Los Angeles bar?According to the complaint filed on Friday in Los Angeles Superior Court, the incident dates back to the evening of February 14. Rosenthal claimed that he was working at Good Times at Davey Wayne's when a group of five people, including Fuqua's daughter, arrived at the bar.He alleged that the group appeared heavily intoxicated and that he refused to allow them entry. According to his complaint, Fuqua's daughter then spat at him, verbally abused him and threatened him. Rosenthal said he eventually asked the group to leave.The complaint further states that around an hour later, Rosenthal spotted Antoine Fuqua outside the bar. The filmmaker allegedly approached him and accused him of pepper-spraying his daughter, a claim Rosenthal denied.Antoine Fuqua and son Brando accused of threatening bar employee with gunsRosenthal has made serious allegations about what happened next. According to his lawsuit, Fuqua pulled out a handgun and struck him in the face. He also accused the director of using racist and antisemitic slurs and threatening to kill him.The complaint further alleges that Fuqua's son, Brando, became involved in the confrontation and swung a handgun towards Rosenthal's face before pointing it at him. Rosenthal claimed that both father and son made him fear for his life before leaving the scene.These claims are part of the lawsuit and have not been established in court.Man seeks $50,000 in damages, claims physical and emotional injuriesIn his lawsuit, Rosenthal is seeking $50,000 in damages and has requested a jury trial. He claimed that the alleged incident left him with serious physical and psychological injuries.The injuries listed in the complaint include a head injury, a fractured nose and cuts to his skin. He also claimed that the injuries could lead to permanent disability.Rosenthal further stated that he had incurred hospital, medical and other expenses following the alleged incident. He is seeking compensation for the financial and emotional impact of the incident.Antoine Fuqua denies all allegationsResponding to the lawsuit, a representative for Fuqua strongly rejected the claims made against the filmmaker."None of the allegations in the complaint are true," the representative told the Daily Mail in a statement on Monday.The publication also reported that it had contacted Rosenthal's lawyers for further comment.No findings have been made against Fuqua or his son in the case, and the allegations will have to be examined through the legal process.Antoine Fuqua's career and Michael Jackson biopicAntoine Fuqua is one of Hollywood's well-known directors and has worked on several successful films, including 'Training Day', 'The Magnificent Seven' and 'The Equalizer' franchise.His recent project was 'Michael', the biographical film based on the life of pop legend Michael Jackson. The film stars Jaafar Jackson, Michael Jackson's nephew, in the lead role, with Colman Domingo and Nia Long portraying his parents, Joseph and Katherine Jackson.The film also features John Logan as its screenwriter. Fuqua's involvement in the project brought renewed attention to the director, whose filmography includes several popular action and drama films.Fuqua is married to actress Lela Rochon, and the couple have two children, Brando and Asia.Get the latest Bollywood & Entertainment News, and more. articles.title: Tidal will start banning AI-generated music next month
articles.summary: Tidal has announced plans to start banning AI-generated music on December 9th. The platform estimates that it will remove 29 million AI songs as a result of the ban.
articles.body: Tidal is officially banning AI-generated music on December 9th. As a result of this change, Tidal will delete around 29 million AI-generated songs and reject an estimated 80,000 to 85,000 tracks per day, according to Tidal music lead Robert Andersen. The move comes just months after Tidal began labeling and demonetizing tracks identified as 100 percent AI-generated. In a post on X, Andersen says Tidal needed to take a more “drastic” measure, as AI music made up 43 percent of the tracks distributed to the platform in the last 90 days. “We believe this will resonate with both artists and listeners alike, as 96% of all AI-generated songs receive zero plays at all,” Andersen adds. Bandcamp similarly banned AI music earlier this year, while other music streaming platforms attempt to address a flood of AI songs by applying new labels or removing them from user algorithms. Spotify recently announced that it removed 50 million AI slop and spam tracks from recommendations over the past year, and also launched new “AI persona” badges for artists that use an AI identity. YouTube has rolled out AI music labels as well, while Apple Music is planning to launch AI labels this year. Meanwhile, Deezer is giving users the option to filter out AI music. “Wholly AI-generated music intended to mislead listeners and impersonate artists is another serious problem that has only increased in scale: It diverts streams and royalties away from the artists, and confuses fans,” Tidal says in a separate post on X. The platform is also going to ban music distributors from submitting AI songs, using the AI detection tool Ircam Amplify and metadata checks to reject submissions generated solely with AI. Tidal notes that it won’t ban songs made with the assistance of AI tools, as long as AI doesn’t make up the “sole output.”

articles.title: David Fincher is being dragged for suspected use of AI in his latest film
articles.summary: Early screenings of the Further Mid-Adventures of Cliff Booth have people convinced that David Fincher is using generative AI.
articles.body: Though David Fincher’s fans had been eagerly anticipating The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, early screenings of the Once Upon a Time in Hollywood sequel starring Brad Pitt have raised questions about whether generative AI was used in the film. People have claimed that the movie is chock-full of uncanny, inconsistent visuals that make it feel more like slop than the sort of polished film you’d expect from the director of sleek productions like Fight Club and The Social Network. Following a number of Cliff Booth critics screenings that took place last week ahead of the film’s premiere on November 25th, moviegoers rushed to social media to lament what they saw. One of the most vocal reactions came from YouTuber / director Patrick Tomasso, who said on X that he walked out of his screening feeling “completely gutted” and that the film featured “some of the most blatant and egregious AI use” he has ever seen from a major studio. Tomasso also insisted you can see AI-generated footage in Cliff Booth’s trailers that have been posted online, and he was confident that Fincher’s latest film is filled with “slop as you know and loathe it. The shit you can pump out of Higgsfield.” Others echoed Tomasso’s sentiments, writing that “the amount of AI in the CLIFF BOOTH movie is astounding to an absurd degree” and vowing to “never watch another Fincher, Pitt or Tarintino [sic] movie again.” Yet some critics enjoyed the film and suggested that the bad AI people thought they were seeing might have actually just been bad CGI. Netflix has neither confirmed nor denied whether AI was used in any capacity to make the film, but Netflix’s heavy involvement in the film’s production and the company’s recent investments in generative AI technology left many suspicious. It did not help that David Fincher, in a recent interview with the Los Angeles Times, responded to questions about his thoughts on AI with “I’m not a Luddite, so I don’t fear the unknown.” Fincher also reasoned that the anti-AI crowd is advocating for artists to stop iterating on their creative processes: “Is everyone satisfied that we have figured this art form out enough that what we really need to do is go back to celluloid? How long have people painted? 40,000 years? We’re talking about a thing that’s a hundred years old and everyone’s going, ‘Stop. Pencils down. No more iterating. It’s not necessary to have at your fingertips the ability to change the color of that person’s eyes.’ Well, it exists. Should we not use it?” The spiel made it sound like he might be jumping on the AI bandwagon. [Media: Set about a decade after Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, Cliff Booth picks up in 1977 at a time when Booth (Pitt) has left his life as a stuntman behind to become a fixer who quietly deals with scandalous problems for Hollywood elites. Cliff still works a number of side gigs as a projectionist and bartender. But the movie is primarily focused on his budding romance with critic-turned-talent agent Karen Crosby (Elizabeth Debicki) and his working relationship with Charlie Peters (Scott Caan), a TV actor who needs Booth’s services to keep his wife (Carla Gugino) from being murdered. At least one trailer for the film features some baffling shots of what looks like people sitting backward in a horse-drawn carriage that make it seem like there might be some generative AI in the mix. It’s hard to tell from the trailers whether that’s actually the case, but in a moment when many creators have been trying to pass off AI generations as human-made art, it’s not surprising that people are suspicious. Netflix has been incorporating AI into its movies and series for some time now, and it seemed like the company was doubling down earlier this year when it acquired Ben Affleck’s startup, InterPositive, for around $600 million. Rather than turning text into visual outputs like many commercially available AI tools, InterPositive’s AI models are designed to generate assets based on footage captured during a film’s production. According to Netflix, InterPositive’s AI was developed with the intention of making it easier to tweak details like lighting or to remove unwanted background elements. The company also made a big deal of emphasizing that InterPositive’s models were highly customizable and well suited to replicating a human director’s signature style. Netflix buying InterPositive and absorbing the company’s development team is part of why there has been so much speculation about AI being used in Cliff Booth. If Cliff Booth actually uses AI and the visuals really are as bad as some have said, it would be a major knock against both Netflix and Fincher — a director known for his meticulous (obsessive, some might argue) attention to detail.

articles.title: Dax Shepard brands college an 'elaborate racket,' predicts tradesmen will get 'last laugh'
articles.summary: Actor Dax Shepard calls higher education a "pretty elaborate racket" over soaring debt pressure, predicting tradesmen will outlast white-collar workers as AI grows.
articles.body: Actor and podcast host Dax Shepard called the American higher education system a "pretty elaborate racket," criticizing soaring tuition costs and the pressure put on middle-class families to take on crushing student debt. Speaking on an episode of the "Armchair Expert" podcast, Shepard rejected the idea that where someone attends college correlates with success. "College has become a pretty elaborate racket," Shepard said in the episode released Monday featuring "Girls" actress Zosia Mamet. "I think the people I work with that have been successful, there's zero correlation between where they went." FOX NEWS POLL: FAITH IN HIGHER EDUCATION IN THE US IS COLLAPSING Shepard added that while he believes higher education can be beneficial, telling middle-class families that their children must go to top-tier, expensive colleges to succeed sends the wrong message. "I think this pressure that middle-class people put on themselves that if their kids don't go to this right school, they're going to be failures, and that they're dying under this pressure and that they're not letting kids in," Shepard said. "I just think it's — become a really f---ed up — the price of it has gotten really expensive." MICHIGAN COLLEGE PRESIDENT URGES 'IT'S INCUMBENT UPON' HIGHER EDUCATION LEADERS TO LOWER TUITION EVERY YEAR While co-host Monica Padman cautioned against suggesting that "education no longer matters," Shepard — who graduated from UCLA — clarified that he "loved [his] education to death." Meanwhile, Mamet pointed out that affordable state schools and community colleges remain valuable alternatives to massive debt. Shepard, who shares two daughters with "Nobody Wants This" actress Kristen Bell, said he won't force his children to go to college and will support them if they choose a different path. SKIP TWO YEARS OF COLLEGE DEBT AND GIVE YOUR FAMILY A LIFETIME OF WEALTH "I've already said numerous times to my daughters, it's like, if you want to go , great, I'll pay. If you don't want to go, and you're on fire for something else that that's not going to help you get to, I'm totally fine with that. I'm not hell-bent on them going to college just because I went," Shepard said. The conversation then turned to what Shepard described as a broader culture of "elitism" stemming from America's shift to a "brain economy" in the 1990s, a dynamic Mamet said looks different across the Atlantic. AI HASN’T REPLACED HUMANS. EMPLOYERS ARE STILL BETTING ON COLLEGE DEGREES Mamet, who has been filming in Wales, said that students in the U.K. are encouraged at the end of high school to choose between college or learning a trade without stigma. She also explained that when she chose not to continue in higher education, she received judgment from a dean at her school as the only student in her graduating class not heading to college. "There's this weird elitism here where we're like, that's somehow lesser than," Mamet said. Shepard agreed, predicting that the rise of artificial intelligence may interrupt that dynamic. "Until AI takes out all the middle-class jobs and the only people who are employed are tradesmen," Shepard quipped. "Then they’ll get the last laugh." Andrew Gillen, a research fellow at the Cato Institute who researches the economics of higher education, told Fox News Digital that the podcast "scratched the surface of a neglected truth." "The sad reality is that a college that provides little in way of an education or that is simply overpriced is too common today," Gillen said. "For example, about 90% of students attend college to improve their financial situation, yet around a quarter to a third of college students are left worse off financially after attending college." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "For this sizable segment, college can be indistinguishable from a racket," he continued. "Having said that, we shouldn’t lose sight of the fact that, for most students, college is a sound investment. When both possible outcomes are acknowledged, it naturally shifts the question from 'College, yes or no’ to ‘which college and which major make sense for me,' which is a much better question, in large part because students and parents that ask it are much less likely to end up making a choice that they regret."
